question: Why should a learning review avoid counterfactual arguments?
text:
In learning reviews and Facilitated Learning Analyses (FLAs), counterfactual arguments—statements asserting that "If person X had done action Y, then outcome Z would not have occurred"[1]—are explicitly avoided for several key reasons:
It fails to explain why actions made sense in the moment: Counterfactual arguments focus on what people did not do rather than understanding why they took the actions they actually did[2][3]. The core goal of a learning review is to uncover how the situation, environment, and conditions made their choices seem logical and appropriate at the time[2][3][4].
It relies on hindsight bias and presumes an unknowable outcome: Counterfactual thinking uses post-event knowledge that was unavailable to the individuals when making decisions[2][5]. Furthermore, counterfactuals assume that investigators can accurately predict an alternate future, whereas it is actually unknowable what would have transpired had a different action been taken[6][7].
It promotes simplistic blame over systemic understanding: Counterfactual reasoning often leads to the flawed conclusion that an event occurred simply because workers failed to follow rules or pay sufficient attention[8]. In reality, discrete shortcuts or omissions occur regularly in normal, successful work[9]; accidents usually result from unexpected combinations of normal performance variability and system conditions rather than individual blunders[10].
It damages trust and psychological safety: Analyzing events through "should have" or "could have" arguments creates judgment and professional embarrassment[1][11]. When employees feel judged rather than understood, trust between the workforce and leadership breaks down, destroying the willingness of participants to share open, honest accounts necessary for organizational learning[12][13].

“Inattention to detail” and “not following procedures” are not root causes even though these are still commonly cited as such in the DOE complex. A root cause is the cause that, if corrected, will prevent recurrence of the event. Human error cannot be eliminated completely—inattention will continue to occur despite our best efforts to eliminate it.
Investigations of events triggered by active error are usually distorted by hindsight—the analyst’s knowledge of facts after the event that were not known, or knowable, by the principal individuals before the event. Hindsight predisposes the analyst to search for data that confirms the apparent shortcomings of the individual(s). Also, explaining what people could have or should have done explains nothing about why they did what they did. 4.chunk: Investigations of accidents or events triggered by active error are usually distorted by hindsight—the analyst’s knowledge of facts after the event that were not known, or possibly even knowable, by the individual(s) involved in the event. In traditional investigations, the investigators interview the people involved after gaining an understanding of the requirements and after becoming very familiar with the details of the event. Hindsight predisposes the investigator to search for information that confirms the individual’s apparent shortcomings. Further, explaining what people could have or should have done says nothing about why they did what they did. Analyzing events from the perspective of “why did the actions taken seem appropriate at the time?” goes a long way to preventing the same thing from happening in the future.

Interviewers should appreciate that the accident participants are also affected by many biases including hindsight bias. Human memory connects images and facts to build a coherent mental story that makes sense in the light of the now known outcome. This is not a conscious process. “Sensemaking” (see definition in glossary)
does not stop after the accident. It is common to interview a firefighter involved in an accident and find their language packed with things they wished they had done differently. Then, in the subsequent weeks, this person’s language changes to the

Gaining a firm understanding of the above concepts will serve you well as you attempt to understand an accident or incident. Remember, if the person involved in the accident had known what the results would be, they probably would have taken a different action. But the future hadn’t happened yet, and they couldn’t have known the outcome. The bottom line is that the human being sitting in front of the interviewer simply did not take the counterfactual action at that time and it is unknowable what would have happened if they had.

In reality, however, most of those discrete omissions or actions occur during the course of normal work continuously. They are not anomalies at all. Indeed, those
same omissions and actions typically lead directly to successful outcomes and even avert disasters. A chance conjunction of events is almost always the difference
between normal success and the rare accident.

The FLA learning product should explain the nature of the accident. The key
commitment of the FLA team is that accidents are not caused by anomalous, blundering, or deviant behavior. Accidents are more accurately understood as unexpected combinations of normal performance variability11 (both human and
system performance variability).

pay homage to the complexities of the work environment in the wake of an accident and instead pretend that the work environment is simple or even complicated, we are not treating our employees fairly or affording them the dignity they deserve.
